_note: The branch's clearest *statutory* (not merely policy-level) confirmation yet of discretionary benefit-setting. The National Pensions Act, 1992 (na-national-pensions-act-1992) does not simply lack a CPI-adjustment clause -- it explicitly assigns amount-setting to ministerial regulation: 'the payment of national pensions including the maximum amount to be paid, the determination of the amount to be paid in any particular case' is set by the Minister 'in consultation with the Minister of Finance' (s.16(1)(b)), with parliamentary approval required only for reductions to aggregate entitlements (s.16(2)). This is a *documented mechanism that is not CPI*, the same shape as Tanzania's PSSSF Act (tz-psssf-act) but at the level of the universal old-age pension itself rather than a public-service occupational fund. The Social Protection Policy 2021-2030 (na-social-protection-policy-2021-2030) shows the resulting asymmetry in practice: its implementation plan sets old-age pension amounts as fixed nominal targets (N$1,300 rising to N$1,350 by 2025/26) with no CPI reference, while explicitly committing only the Child Grant to inflation-related adjustment ('adjustments will be made to the existing amount of the Child Grants to account for inflationary losses over time') -- the Policy names a mechanism for one grant and is silent on it for the other, rather than being silent on both. A genuine point of contrast with Tanzania and Botswana: the ISSA/SSA country profile here (2024-07 vintage, https://www.issa.int/sites/default/files/documents/2024-07/Namibia.pdf, not minted as a corpus node per the branch's standing precedent) is *consistent* with the primary sources rather than conflicting with them -- 'Not legally mandated. The benefit amount is reviewed and adjusted on an ad hoc basis' -- so this slice has no three-way (or two-way) documented conflict to report, only convergent confirmation from a statute, a policy and a secondary compilation.

_open_questions.question: The NSA's own CPI bulletin (August 2025) names neither COICOP nor an index formula (Laspeyres, Jevons, geometric mean, etc.) -- unlike Botswana's and Tanzania's methodology documents, which state both explicitly. A dedicated NSA 'concepts and methods' or technical report, if one exists, was searched for but not located this session; nsa.org.na's own /inflation/ page carries no link to one.

The NCPI is still on a December 2012 base (rebased 2013 using the 2009/10 Household Income and Expenditure Survey) as of the August 2025 bulletin -- 13 years on the same base. NSA's own site announces it will 'conduct the 2025/2026 Namibia Household Income & Expenditure Survey (NHIES)'. Whether a rebasing using that new survey has since occurred was not checked further this session.

The Social Protection Policy 2021-2030 commits only the Child Grant to inflation-loss compensation, not the Old Age Pension. Whether a newer policy revision or implementation report (2022-2026) has since extended a similar formal commitment to the Old Age Pension was not checked this session.

The Government Institutions Pension Fund (GIPF, established 1989) is Namibia's civil-service occupational pension fund -- the likely Namibian analogue to Tanzania's Public Service Social Security Fund (tz-psssf-act) -- but is entirely distinct from the universal National Pensions Act scheme researched this session. Not researched at all this session; gipf.com.na was found in search but not fetched.

reports.title: Namibia Consumer Price Index (NCPI) Bulletin
reports.description: UPDATE 2026-08-13 (AF/G.23, reconfirmed CPI-methodology-citation gap persists as of the June 2026 bulletin; no COICOP/SADC Harmonised CPI/IMF-ILO CPI Manual reference found after additional search paths, including nsa.org.na's wp-json REST search API -- see na-g23-municipal.json's _dropped for detail): Namibia's official monthly Consumer Price Index release. VERIFIED DIRECTLY this session via the August 2025 bulletin: base period 'Dec 2012=100', the basket having been 'last rebased in 2013, using household expenditure data collected in the 2009/10 Household Income and Expenditure Survey'; the current basket 'contains over 350 items' organised into '12 categories and 55 sub-categories', with prices 'collected monthly from more than 900 retail outlets'; published 'approximately 15 days after the end of the reference month'; coverage stated as 'national, urban and rural households of all income groups'. Neither COICOP nor a named index formula (Laspeyres, Jevons, geometric mean, etc.) appears in this bulletin -- a genuine absence, not an oversight of this session's reading, and distinct from Botswana's and Tanzania's methodology documents, which both name their formula explicitly (see _open_questions).

release_schedule.note: NSA publishes the NCPI bulletin monthly with no published release calendar found on the site. Observed pattern from the document archive: June 2026 bulletin published 2026-07-09, May 2026 bulletin published 2026-06-11, April 2026 bulletin published 2026-05-12 (each roughly in the second week of the month following the reference month). As of 2026-08-11 the July 2026 bulletin had not yet appeared (URL guess for it 404'd), so it is expected imminently based on this pattern; August 2026 bulletin would follow a month later.

reports.title: National Pensions Act, 1992 (Act No. 10 of 1992)
reports.publisher: Government of the Republic of Namibia
reports.description: Namibia's foundational statute for the universal old-age pension, read section-by-section this session via NamibLII. VERIFIED DIRECTLY. Purpose: 'to provide for national pensions to be paid to aged, blind and disabled persons' (Social Protection Policy 2021-2030's own citation of the Act, p.15, s.5.3, quoted verbatim: 'The National Pensions Act, 1992 (No. 10 of 1992), provides for national pensions to be paid to aged, visually impaired and persons with disability, and to provide for matters incidental thereto'). On amount-setting, s.16(1)(b) assigns 'the payment of national pensions including the maximum amount to be paid, the determination of the amount to be paid in any particular case' to ministerial regulation; s.16(3) permits 'different pensions to be paid to different categories of aged persons according to their income and other assets'; s.16(2) requires parliamentary approval only for reductions to aggregate pension entitlements. The Minister acts 'in consultation with the Minister of Finance'. No section ties any amount to the Consumer Price Index or any price index -- the mechanism is explicitly ministerial/regulatory discretion, not an absence of a stated mechanism.

reports.title: Social Protection Policy 2021-2030
reports.publisher: Ministry of Gender Equality, Poverty Eradication and Social Welfare (Namibia)
reports.description: Namibia's national social protection policy, adopted by Cabinet Decision No. 4th/23.03.21/009, March 2021. VERIFIED DIRECTLY this session. Section 5.3 (p.15) lists ten governing acts as the 'National Policy Frameworks', naming the National Pensions Act, 1992 first among them (na-national-pensions-act-1992). The implementation plan sets old-age pension values as fixed nominal targets -- 'N$1 300 (2020)' rising to 'N$1 350' by 2025/26 -- rather than a formula. The document commits only the Child Grant to inflation-linked language: 'adjustments will be made to the existing amount of the Child Grants to account for inflationary losses over time'; the equivalent language is absent for the old-age pension anywhere in the document. Elsewhere: 'The old-age pension has the best adequacy, covering 65% of the extremely poor consumption expenditure.' No section names the Consumer Price Index, inflation rates, or the Namibia Statistics Agency as an input for setting the old-age pension specifically.
